cards.title: Resetting the system
cards.author: Zahid Hussain
cards.why: This is crucial for understanding current constitutional debates and the governance challenges surrounding administrative restructuring in Pakistan.
cards.summary: The author examines the recent government proposal to hold a referendum on creating new provinces in Pakistan. The article critiques the move as a potential attempt to bypass constitutional processes and warns that it may cause political instability. It highlights the lack of a clear, unified blueprint among political parties regarding administrative restructuring.
key_facts: The interior minister has suggested a referendum to approve the creation of new provinces.
The PPP has officially rejected any move to divide the province of Sindh.
The PML-N has yet to adopt a formal position on the administrative restructuring plan.
The author warns that a simple yes or no referendum may aggravate political instability.

vocab.meaning: A process that generates many unforeseen and complicated problems.
The outline or shape of something.

text: THE issue of administrative restructuring is back on the political agenda. The interior minister has called for a referendum to seek public approval for the creation of new provinces, arguing that the existing system of governance has “collapsed” and needs a fundamental reset.
In recent months, this contentious issue has been discussed at seminars and other public forums, while political leaders have voiced their individual opinions.

The idea of holding a referendum on such a complex issue is apparently being floated to bypass the constitutional process. Coming from the interior minister, the proposal leaves little ambiguity about whose plan it is. Securing parliamentary approval for a referendum may not be difficult in a pliant house. But can a simple “yes” or “no” referendum resolve the intricate and politically sensitive question of creating new administrative units?

There are certainly compelling reasons to restructure the existing provinces to improve governance. But the approach now being pursued is likely to open a Pandora’s box, creating chaos and further aggravating political instability. Several proposals for creating new administrative units may be circulating, but no political party has come forward with a concrete blueprint.

While the PPP has rejected any move to divide Sindh or create new administrative units in the province, the ruling PML-N has yet to adopt an official position, although individual ministers have expressed their views.

There has been an intriguing silence on the issue from Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Nawaz Sharif. Not surprisingly, the smaller coalition partners , widely seen as close to the powers that be, have emerged as strong supporters of the restructuring plan, despite its contours remaining unclear.

The question of administrative restructuring cannot be divorced from the broader democratic process. Mr Naqvi, himself a product of a system whose legitimacy remains contested, argues that a referendum is part of democracy. “We all talk about democracy. Parliamentarians represent the people of Pakistan. I request all political parties to consider that most survey reports suggest that new provinces should be created for better governance,” he maintains.
Good governance requires rule of law, constitutional supremacy and accountable institutions.

Indeed, an elected parliament represents the will of the people and, in a democratic system, is the supreme legislative body mandated to initiate such changes. Yet, in this case, the debate on a major constitutional issue has not begun in parliament but has instead been initiated from outside it. Has there been any meaningful debate on this critical matter in the legislature, however contested its legitimacy?

The interior minister’s appeal to political parties to take note of “survey reports” favouring the creation of new provinces is equally questionable. Opinion polls may offer some indication of public sentiment, but they cannot serve as the basis for constitutional change.

Moreover, we know how limited in scope and reach many such surveys are in Pakistan. Has the minister also taken note of the numerous other surveys reflecting public dissatisfaction with the existing political order?

More importantly, the Constitution clearly lays down the procedure for creating new provinces. The proposal for a referendum appears designed to circumvent these constitutional provisions. The Constitution also prescribes a well-defined procedure for its own amendment. There can be no shortcut to such a fundamental change.

The 18th Amendment provides a useful example. It altered almost one-third of the Constitution, but only after nearly 18 months of intensive deliberations by a multiparty parliamentary committee, which eventually forged a consensus. Why cannot the same democratic and parliamentary process be followed for an issue of such national importance, rather than seeking to resolve it through a referendum?

There is much talk about resetting a system of governance that has supposedly collapsed. There can be little disagreement that the country’s political and governance structures are deeply dysfunctional and require fundamental reform if Pakistan is to move forward. It is odd, however, that the rhetoric of resetting the system comes from those who are themselves equally responsible for its present state.
Governance cannot be improved merely by creating new provinces. It requires, above all, a system founded on the rule of law, constitutional supremacy and accountable democratic institutions.

Those now championing administrative restructuring and a reset are also responsible for undermining the democratic process and curtailing judicial independence through the 26th and 27th Amendments , further eroding the Constitution’s fundamental principles.

With democratic freedoms increasingly constrained, the country is moving towards authoritarianism. Creating new provinces or redrawing administrative boundaries will do little to improve governance or rescue a collapsing system in such circumstances.

Phrases such as “resetting the system” and “referendum” are familiar instruments. Military rulers in the past have used similar language to consolidate their power and legitimise authoritarian rule. This time, too, the signs are hardly reassuring. The exercise looks less like a genuine attempt at reform and more like an effort to salvage a failing system through cosmetic adjustments.

There has also been talk of a 28th Constitutional amendment. While the contours of the proposed amendment remain unclear, indications are that it could further tighten political control while incorporating administrative restructuring into a broader package of changes. This raises serious questions about the real objectives behind the proposed reforms.

There is certainly an urgent need to break with the status quo and restore the democratic process. But that is not the kind of reset Mohsin Naqvi and others appear to be advocating. Neither a proposed referendum nor an impending 28th amendment, pursued outside a genuinely democratic process, is likely to bring political stability.

What Pakistan needs is political stability built on constitutional supremacy, democratic freedoms and strong, independent institutions. Administrative restructuring may well be part of the solution, but it must emerge from an open, inclusive and constitutionally mandated democratic process — not be imposed from outside it.
The writer is an author and journalist.

cards.title: Not another Yalta
cards.author: Mahir Ali
cards.why: It provides a contemporary perspective on the shifting dynamics of global power and the limits of summit-level diplomacy in a modern geopolitical context.
cards.summary: This column compares the historical Yalta Conference of 1945 to a modern-day trilateral summit in Shenzhen between the US, Russia, and China. It notes that unlike the foundational peace architecture of the post-WWII era, the current summit lacks a clear agenda and serves more as a political spectacle. The author highlights the complexity of the Iran war, which remains a key point of tension for the participating powers.
key_facts: The Yalta Conference took place in February 1945 with the leaders of the USSR, US, and UK.
China has reduced its reliance on Iranian crude oil imports.
China has substantially increased its exports of green technology like solar panels.
The Shenzhen summit agenda includes discussions on strategic stability in major-power relations.

vocab.meaning: To act in a way to impress onlookers.
A military tactic where an enemy is attacked simultaneously from two sides.

text: WHEN the leaders of the USSR, US and UK gathered at a Crimean resort in Feb 1945 for a weeklong trilateral summit, an extensive agenda awaited them. With the Nazis caught in a pincer movement between the rapidly advancing Red Army and its western allies, the European segment of the world war had entered its endgame. The architecture of peace needed to be sketched out.

Historians still argue about whether Franklin Roosevelt and Winston Churchill conceded too much to Joseph Stalin in delineating ‘spheres of influence’, but it was indisputably a momentous occasion. For better or worse, many of the decisions made at Yalta endured for decades, and some still resonate. No comparable outcome can be imagined from this week’s summit in Shenzhen.

It may well turn out to be little more than a grandiose photo-op. A domineering presence on the global stage has additional appeal for Donald Trump following his domestic humiliation in the midterm elections . Vladimir Putin is inevitably keen to be counted among the ‘Big 3’. By many accounts, Xi Jinping is a reluctant host — perhaps partly because there’s only a vague agenda — “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”, according to Beijing. And he’s naturally wary of Trump’s tendency to grandstand.
The Iran war could figure in discussions at Shenzhen.

The Iran war is expected to figure in the discussions. Some good could possibly come out of that if both Xi and Putin urge the US president to recognise the error of his ways. The conflict is particularly painful for China, given its reliance on Iranian crude.

On the brighter side, China’s oil imports have decreased by design, while exports of its cutting-edge green tech — including solar panels — have substantially increased. Russia, on the other hand, has been delighted by a sanctions reprieve and a surge in petroleum exports, largely due to the transport hiatus in the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits. Besides, the US/Israeli conflict helps Russia portray its war against Ukraine as a comparable venture aimed at safeguarding its security. Moscow’s stance makes slightly more sense than the justifications from Washington and Tel Aviv for their aggression against Iran. China sees both wars as huge strategic errors.

Trump seems to believe the Israeli propaganda that Tehran must be prevented from acquiring a nuclear weapon, an outcome that now logically seems likelier than it did before the attacks. That may help to explain why nuclear proliferation was among the topics he hoped to broach at his talks with Xi and Putin. Back in February, his administration turned down Moscow’s proposal to extend a strategic arms reduction treaty, with Trump aspiring for a new deal that includes China, whose expanding nuclear arsenal appears to have alarmed Sinophobes in the US. Given that even its projected stockpiles are a fraction of what’s stored in Russian and American silos, Beijing does not wish to play ball.

Shortly before flying to Asia, Trump noted that denuclearisation, Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite topic, Ukraine” would be up for discussion. Volodymyr Zelensky is alarmed by the possibilities, but a carve-up without Kyiv at the table is hardly likely. China sees Ukraine as a European issue that should be discussed at a more appropriate forum. Trump is disinclined, meanwhile, to bring up the Nvidia fiasco after the US chip-maker’s CEO Jensen Huang was ousted over revelations about an affair with a purported Chinese ‘asset’.

America rem­ains determined to deny China superiority in artificial intelligence throu­­gh curbs on chip exports. But that’s probably another lost battle. Exactly what the three lea­ders will talk about remains to be seen.

Climate change won’t be on the agenda. That’s being thrashed out at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, where there’s no official US representation, given the Trump administration’s focus on exacerbating global heating despite rapidly mounting evidence about its catastrophic consequences, from the devastation in Nepal caused by glacier collapse to an estimated 50,000 heatwave deaths in Europe during a scorching summer, not to mention the ecocidal aspect of the Pales­tinian genocide as well as the Iranian, Ukrainian and Sudanese conflicts. Not to mention the ginormous carbon footprint of proliferating US data centres.

As Swedish activist Greta Thunberg accurately spelt it out in Antalya, “The planet is not dying, it is being killed.” And the outgoing UN Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, was equally correct in pointing out: “It’s make or bake time.” He might have erred, though, in comparing fossil fuels to dinosaurs and claiming the latter “did not have a lobby”. They do, and some of its components might be congregating in Shenzhen right now.

cards.title: Predatory medicine
cards.author: Murad Moosa Khan
cards.why: It sheds light on the socio-economic challenges within the healthcare sector, which is a relevant theme for public policy and governance discussions.
cards.summary: This piece discusses the ethical shift in modern healthcare from patient-centric care to profit-driven models, referred to as 'predatory medicine.' It explores how commercial interests can lead to unnecessary medical procedures and inflated costs. The author argues that healthcare systems must prioritize humanism and ethics over financial gain to remain legitimate.
key_facts: The book Predatory Medicine by cardiologist Jack Vangrow explores how healthcare can become an extractive enterprise.
Predatory medical practices include unnecessary investigations and avoidable surgical procedures.
Commercialisation in medicine becomes unethical when profit takes precedence over patient wellbeing.

vocab.meaning: Designed to take resources out for gain, often unfairly.
